validated_results.title: Effects of beta-carotene supplementation on cancer incidence by baseline characteristics in the Physicians' Health Study (United States).
validated_results.reason: Randomized trial of beta-carotene supplementation reporting incident prostate cancer risk in US male physicians.

extraction.comparison_type: beta-carotene 50 mg on alternate days versus placebo
extraction.timing: prospective randomized follow-up of nearly 13 years

sample_size.excerpt: The Physicians' Health Study (PHS) was a randomized trial of beta-carotene (50 mg, alternate days) and aspirin in primary prevention of cancer and cardiovascular disease among 22,071 US male physicians.

cases.excerpt: 2667 incident cancers were confirmed, with 1117 prostate, 267 colon, and 178 lung cancers.

effect_size.excerpt: There were no significant differences with supplementation in total (relative risk (RR) = 1.0, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 0.9-1.0); prostate (RR = 1.0, 95% CI = 0.9-1.1); colon (RR = 0.9, 95% CI = 0.7-1.2); or lung (RR = 0.9, 95% CI = 0.7-1.2) cancer, and no differences over time.

confidence_interval.excerpt: There were no significant differences with supplementation in total (relative risk (RR) = 1.0, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 0.9-1.0); prostate (RR = 1.0, 95% CI = 0.9-1.1); colon (RR = 0.9, 95% CI = 0.7-1.2); or lung (RR = 0.9, 95% CI = 0.7-1.2) cancer, and no differences over time.

comparison.excerpt: There were no significant differences with supplementation in total (relative risk (RR) = 1.0, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 0.9-1.0); prostate (RR = 1.0, 95% CI = 0.9-1.1)

design.excerpt: The Physicians' Health Study (PHS) was a randomized trial of beta-carotene (50 mg, alternate days) and aspirin
